spec.credit: UPSC CSE (Main) 2023 · General Studies Paper II · Q12
spec.text: Explain the constitutional perspectives of Gender Justice with the help of relevant Constitutional Provisions and case laws.

scenes.vo: UPSC, twenty twenty-three. General Studies Paper Two, fifteen marks, two hundred and fifty words. Explain the constitutional perspectives of gender justice, with provisions and case laws. Here's the strange part. The same Article both bars and allows special treatment for women.

spec.text: Explain the constitutional perspectives of Gender Justice with the help of relevant Constitutional Provisions and case laws.

scenes.vo: Read what it asks. Explain means a clear account, no argument needed. And there are two named jobs: provisions, and case laws. We add two more. Statutes and figures. Then a balanced close.

lines.text: Article fifteen one bars discrimination on grounds of sex.
Article fifteen three allows special provision for women.
That is the idea of substantive equality.

scenes.vo: Start with the rule. Article fifteen one bars discrimination on grounds of sex. Article fifteen three allows special provision for women. Both stand together. That is the idea of substantive equality.

lines.text: The other provisions fill in the rest.
Equal pay for equal work in Article thirty-nine.
And one-third seats for women in Panchayats and Municipalities.

scenes.vo: The other provisions fill in the rest. Article fourteen, equality. Article twenty-one, dignity. Equal pay for equal work in Article thirty-nine. And one-third seats for women in Panchayats and Municipalities.

lines.text: But text needs courts to give it life.
In nineteen ninety-seven, Vishaka laid down workplace guidelines because no law existed.
Parliament passed the POSH Act in twenty thirteen.

scenes.vo: But text needs courts to give it life. In nineteen ninety-seven, Vishaka laid down workplace guidelines because no law existed. Parliament passed the POSH Act in twenty thirteen.

lines.text: In Joseph Shine, in twenty eighteen, section four ninety-seven fell.
In Nitisha, in twenty twenty-one, indirect discrimination was recognised.
Law moved from protection to autonomy.

scenes.vo: But cases moved further. In Joseph Shine, in twenty eighteen, section four ninety-seven fell. In Nitisha, in twenty twenty-one, indirect discrimination was recognised. Law moved from protection to autonomy.

blocks.text: Gender justice means equality in law and in fact. The Constitution bars discrimination on sex in _Article 15(1)_ yet permits special provision for women in Article 15(3).
1. Constitutional provisions

• _Equality_: Articles 14, 15(1) and 16(1)-(2). • _Dignity_: Article 21; Article 23(1) bars traffic in human beings. • _Directive Principles_: 39(d) equal pay for equal work; Article 42, just and humane conditions of work. • Duty: 51A(e). • Politics: one-third of seats in Panchayats and Municipalities (243D, 243T); the 106th Amendment adds one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats after delimitation.
2. Case laws

• _Vishaka_ (1997): workplace guidelines until a law was made. • _Anuj Garg_ (2007): a ban on women in bars failed Articles 14, 15 and 19(1)(g). • _Joseph Shine_ (2018): section 497 IPC, adultery, struck down. • _Babita Puniya_ (2020): permanent commission for women officers; _Nitisha_ (2021): indirect discrimination recognised.
A timeline of the five cases.
blocks.label: Fig. 1: From protection to equal treatment

blocks.text: 3. Laws and figures

• The POSH Act, 2013: every employer must set up an Internal Committee led by a senior woman. • Maternity leave rose from 12 to 26 weeks (2017). • Female labour force participation rose from 23.3 per cent in 2017-18 to 41.7 per cent in 2023-24.
4. Weighing it
So law has moved from protecting women to securing their autonomy and equal outcomes. Yet reserved seats in legislatures await delimitation: text and practice still differ.

scenes.vo: Now we write. Two hundred and fifty words, about eleven minutes. Open with Article fifteen. One line holds both the bar and the exception.

scenes.vo: Section three is the follow-through. The POSH Act. Maternity leave of twenty-six weeks. And women's labour participation, up from twenty-three point three to forty-one point seven per cent.

weak.text: Article 15(3) means women cannot be treated equally.
weak.miss: 15(3) permits special provision; 15(1) still bars discrimination

weak.text: Mary Roy v State of Kerala was decided under Article 14.
weak.miss: it is a statutory ruling on the Succession Act, 1925

weak.text: The Vishaka guidelines are still the only law on workplace harassment.
weak.miss: the 2013 POSH Act now sets the law

weak.text: Women's reservation in Parliament is already in force.
weak.miss: it takes effect only after delimitation

scenes.vo: Close with a balance, then see the easy answer. It treats Article fifteen three as unequal treatment. It says Mary Roy was an Article fourteen case. It is a ruling on succession law. It calls Vishaka the only law, and it names no cases.
